alt: Field lines leave the north pole of a bar magnet and curve round to the south pole without crossing, closest together at the poles where the field is strongest; compass needles line up along them. Below, unlike poles attract and like poles repel, and iron, nickel, cobalt and steel are magnetic while copper, aluminium, brass and plastic are not.
caption: Field lines run from N to S, never cross, and crowd together where the field is strongest.

alt: End-on views of a wire: current out of the page gives anticlockwise circular field lines, current into the page gives clockwise ones, by the right-hand grip rule. A solenoid wound on a soft iron core has a field like a bar magnet outside and a strong, nearly uniform field inside. More current, more turns and a soft iron core make an electromagnet stronger.
caption: Coil a current-carrying wire round soft iron and you get a magnet you can switch off.

alt: A table: 20 turns at 1.0 A lifts 4 paperclips, 40 turns at 1.0 A lifts 9, and 40 turns at 2.0 A lifts 17. Rows 1 and 2 change only the turns, showing more turns gives a stronger magnet; rows 2 and 3 change only the current, showing more current does. Rows 1 and 3 change both, so they are not a fair test.
caption: Compare only rows where one variable changes.

alt: Fleming’s left-hand rule: first finger points along the field from N to S, second finger along the current and the thumb gives the motion, all at right angles. A wire carrying current into the page between a north pole on the left and a south pole on the right is pushed downwards. Reversing the current or field reverses the force; there is no force when the wire is parallel to the field.
caption: Field, current and force are mutually at right angles; Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the direction.

alt: A magnet and a coil joined to a centre-zero meter. Pushing the magnet in deflects the needle one way, holding it still gives zero and pulling it out deflects the needle the other way. Moving faster, a stronger magnet or more turns give a bigger induced voltage; a generator’s turning coil produces alternating current.
caption: Only a changing field induces a voltage; reverse the change and the voltage reverses.

alt: A transverse wave drawn about a rest line, with the wavelength marked crest to crest and the amplitude from rest to trough; examples are water, rope and electromagnetic waves. Below, a longitudinal wave with compressions and rarefactions, one wavelength from compression to compression; sound is longitudinal and needs a medium.
caption: Transverse waves vibrate across the direction of travel; longitudinal waves vibrate along it.

alt: Left: a ray reflects from a mirror with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal. Right: a ray enters a glass block, slows down and bends towards the normal, then speeds up and bends away from the normal as it leaves. Frequency is unchanged, so light of 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz has a wavelength of 600 nm in air and 400 nm in glass.
caption: Refraction is a change of speed; the frequency never changes.

alt: Seven regions in order of decreasing wavelength and increasing frequency and energy: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, each with a use and a main hazard. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising. All are transverse, need no medium and travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.
caption: Moving down the spectrum, wavelength falls and frequency and energy rise, so the hazard grows.
